messages.text: I'll stay here.
All right. I'll follow you.
I trusted you.
You asked me to follow you, not fear you.
I'm done talking. Stay away.
I'm too angry to talk.
I'm busy right now.
I'm no longer available.
The conversation has ended.
I am not sure how to answer that.
I cannot trade right now.
I refuse to trade with you.
I cannot show you that right now.
I don't know you well enough for that.
I cannot accept gifts right now.
Keep your distance.
I should ask a grown-up before taking that.
I cannot accept that.
There is nothing there.
I cannot help right now.
I cannot be hired yet.
I do not know how to trade yet.
I have no trades available.
They stare at you, unsure what to say.
Mmph... let me sleep.
Come back when the sun is up.
I already woke up once for you tonight.
You've bothered me enough for one night.
My bed! What is wrong with you?
That was my bed. I will remember this.
That was mean. I am telling someone.
You know, you're not so bad to talk to.
It's good to speak with someone who listens.
I should have known better than to speak with you.
Careful. Villages remember cruelty.
You've asked enough questions for one day.
I have work to do. Ask something else.
Enough of that for now.
Try something else. My patience has limits.
Hmph. Maybe don't quit your day job.
Still thinking about the {gift_item} you gave me. That was a real kindness.
That {gift_item} you gave me was useful. Thank you again.
I am still deciding what to do with that {gift_item} you gave me.
I remember that {gift_item}. Not fondly.
I have not forgotten the {gift_item} you handed me.
I heard you gave {villager_name} {gift_item}. That was kind of you.
{villager_name} seemed pleased with that {gift_item}.
I heard about the {gift_item} you gave {villager_name}. Interesting choice.
{villager_name} did not sound pleased about that {gift_item}.
I heard what you gave {villager_name}. Do not bring that sort of thing here.
This is wonderful. You chose like someone who knows me.
{gift_item} is a welcome gift.
A curious gift. I will think about it.
I do not have much use for {gift_item}.
That is an insult, not a gift.
{gift_item}? For my work? That is thoughtful.
I can make good use of {gift_item}.
Thank you. I suppose this has its uses.
{gift_item} is a poor match for my trade.
Do not bring danger and call it a present.
About that gift advice... good. {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}. Word gets around when a tip lands.
So {gift_item} worked for {tested_villager}. I am glad my advice held up.
About that gift advice... hm. If {gift_item} did not suit {gift_subject}, try {alternative_gift} instead.
That one soured? Then bring {alternative_gift} next time. {gift_subject} should take that more kindly.
Did they? Hm. Maybe {gift_subject} would prefer {alternative_gift}. Or maybe they were in a mood.
So {gift_item} went badly. Try {alternative_gift} if you want my better guess.
Advice is not a promise. Still, {alternative_gift} should go over better with {gift_subject}.
You came back to blame me? Try {alternative_gift} next time and call it even.
Maybe I misremembered. Maybe you asked the wrong person. Either way, {alternative_gift} is safer.
Well, now you know. {gift_item} is not the way to win over {gift_subject}. Try {alternative_gift}.
That advice turned sideways. Bring {alternative_gift} and you may get a kinder answer.
I lost the thread of that gift advice.
Here. Take {gift_item}. You have earned a little kindness back.
I wanted you to have {gift_item}. Good neighbors share what they can.
{gift_item} should serve you well. Consider it thanks from this village.
So the {gift_item} was only kindness on loan?
You gave me {gift_item}, then took it back. I will remember both parts.
A gift loses its warmth when it walks away in your hands.
That {gift_item} was not yours to take.
Taking another person's gift from my keeping is a poor kind of bold.
I know what was given to me. I also know who just took it.
I caught wind of different land {vague_direction}. Could be worth a walk.
I caught wind of {target_article} {vague_direction}.
I caught wind of {target_article} about {distance} {direction}.
I keep hearing stories about {target_article} somewhere {vague_direction}{vertical}.
I keep hearing about {target_article} around {distance} {direction}{vertical}.
Here. I marked {target_article} on this map. It should sit about {distance} {direction}{vertical}.
Bring me news after you walk the place I mentioned.
I am not sure which story you mean.
So {target_article} was really there. Good. A rumor is lighter once it has footprints under it.
You reached {target_article}? Then the old talk had a road in it after all.
You found {target_article}. Then there are neighbors beyond the story, not just smoke and guessing.
{target_article}, truly? Then the road between here and there matters now.
Another village at {target_article}. That is not a landmark, that is people.
Good. If {target_article} is real, then so are its doors, its fields, and its worries.
You reached {target_article}. I hope they greeted you better than the wilderness did.
{target_article}, confirmed. Old stone is easier to respect when someone comes back from it.
So {target_article} was not just campfire talk. Careful with places that outlive their builders.
You found {target_article}. I suppose old stone still knows how to call travelers in.
{target_article}. Hm. Some thresholds should be crossed with one foot ready to leave.
Then the tale about {target_article} had teeth after all. I am glad they did not close on you.
You reached {target_article} and returned. Some rumors are warnings wearing roofs.
{target_article}, found. There are houses that shelter folk, and houses that watch them.
You came back from {target_article}. That alone says the rumor deserved respect.
So {target_article} stands where they said. Some doors are better confirmed from outside.
{target_article}. I will remember that name with the kind of caution it deserves.
{target_article}, beneath the water. I will believe the waves were telling the truth this once.
You found {target_article}? The sea hides things, but apparently not from you.
{target_article}, confirmed. I do not trust water that keeps architecture.
Then the rumor sank deep and stayed true. That is rare.
You reached {target_article}. I hope the water let you leave with all your thoughts intact.
You found {target_article}. Timber below ground always means a story went too deep.
{target_article}, then. The ground remembers every hand that tried to hollow it out.
You found {target_article}. Listen twice before trusting old supports.
So the beams were real. Places like {target_article} always sound tired.
{target_article}. That is a road made by people who forgot roads should see daylight.
{target_article}. Keep that story quiet. Some places should not hear their own names.
You came back from {target_article}. Speak softly. Even memory might echo down there.
{target_article}, confirmed. That is not a discovery I would celebrate loudly.
So the deep rumor was true. Some truths are best carried carefully.
You found {target_article}. I hope you left more silence there than you took.
{target_article}, then. That is not just a rumor. That is a door waiting under the world.
You found {target_article}. Some stone does not mark a place; it marks a question.
{target_article}, confirmed. I wonder how long it has been waiting for footsteps.
So the path led to {target_article}. That sounds less like a destination than a warning.
You reached {target_article}. Some roads go outward. That one pulls down.
You found {target_article} and came back. I will not ask what the heat sounded like.
{target_article}, real enough to find and harsh enough to remember.
You confirmed {target_article}. Some places make even a rumor smell of smoke.
So {target_article} was there. Good. I prefer knowing where the dangerous roads start.
You came back from {target_article}. I would call that lucky, skilled, or both.
{target_article}. Good to know. A warned road is kinder than an unwarned one.
You found {target_article}. Then we know which horizon to mistrust.
{target_article}, confirmed. Towers are louder than they look.
So the patrol stories were true. Best to know where trouble keeps a roof.
You reached {target_article}. I hope they saw less of you than you saw of them.
You found {target_article}. Ruins always have more memory than walls.
{target_article}, then. Broken places still know how to keep secrets.
You confirmed {target_article}. The past is never quite as empty as it pretends.
So {target_article} was real. I wonder what story broke there first.
You reached {target_article}. Some places are leftovers, but not harmless ones.
{target_article}. Sounds like the rumor was testing your judgment before the place did.
You found {target_article}. Whoever built it trusted challenge more than comfort.
{target_article}, confirmed. A place like that does not invite travelers. It measures them.
So the tale of {target_article} was true. I hope you brought back more than bruises.
You reached {target_article}. I would call that brave, but brave and foolish share a fence.
You found {target_article}. Good. The story has somewhere solid to stand now.
{target_article}, confirmed. I will pass that along with fewer maybes.
You reached {target_article}. A place is different once someone here has seen it.
So the rumor had bones under it. Good to know.
{target_article}. I will remember the name with a little more certainty now.
You found the place I mentioned. Good. I will remember that.

openings.text: You must be new here. What brings you to our village?
I haven't seen you before. What brings you here?
You must be new here. Are you visiting?
I haven't seen you before. Are you new?
Good to see you. What can I do for you?
Hi! Did you come to visit?
Um. Are you here to talk?
I can listen, but then I am going back inside.

closings.text: I am going to find someone older.

lines.text: Thank you for bringing me back near home. A short road feels longer when the night has teeth.
I came back in one piece. That is the kind of help people remember.
I made it back, but not cleanly. Next time, we move slower or fight sooner.
I am glad to be home, but I am still feeling that road. Do not mistake thanks for forgetting.
You asked me to follow, then turned your hand against me. That is not a small thing.
I followed because I thought you meant to protect me. Now I know to measure that promise twice.
Back without a dent worth naming. I will call that a good fit.
There are marks on me I would rather see on a breastplate. Next time, let the metal take it.
I know the sound of a bad strike. Yours was worse because I trusted the hand behind it.
We came back with all our pieces where they belong. Good enough for my ledger.
I know a shallow cut from a deep mistake. That trip had a little of both.
I expect sharp things at work. I did not expect one from the person I followed.
A clean route out and a clean route back. I could ink that with a steady hand.
That path needs a red mark on the map. I would rather not limp through it twice.
I can redraw a bad map. Redrawing trust is harder.
I returned with breath steady and prayers unused. That is a blessing I will not waste.
I can tend the hurt, but I would rather not collect it on the way home.
A wound from an enemy is simple. A wound from a guide asks harder questions.
Home before the rows missed me. Thank you for seeing me back to the village.
I have worked through worse aches, but I should not need a harvest of bruises from one trip.
Trust grows slowly. You cut yours down fast.
A clean return, no snags. I like a trip that ends like a well-tied line.
Something got its hook in me out there. Next time, we cut the line sooner.
I know bait when I see it now. Do not ask me to bite twice.
Straight out, straight back. A good route flies true.
That trip feathered wrong. I came home, but not without a bend in the shaft.
You loosed that hurt at close range. I will remember the aim.
Boots dusty, soles whole. That is how I like returning.
I can patch leather. Patching myself is worse work.
You split trust like old hide. It will not soften quickly.
A journey with a tidy ending. I appreciate a chapter that closes at home.
That outing needs a margin note: return achieved, judgment questionable.
I have read warnings with kinder endings than the one you wrote for me.
Solid trip, solid return. Foundations matter.
I came back chipped. A wall can take that. A person should not have to.
You cracked something load-bearing between us.
Home with no one missing. That is the whole job, really.
I am back in the fold, but I was not guarded as carefully as I hoped.
A shepherd who strikes the flock earns no easy trust.
Good work has a clean finish. Getting me home counts.
That trip handled poorly. I felt every bad grip on the way back.
A tool used wrong can still be repaired. Trust is less forgiving.
You brought me back without needing the worst of it. Restraint is a weapon too.
I came back marked. Next time, keep the edge between us and danger.
I respect sharp steel. I do not respect turning it on someone who followed you.
I do not have a trade for it yet, but coming home safely feels like honest work.
I was looking for direction, not bruises. Still, I made it back.
I followed because I thought you knew where we were going. I was wrong about more than the road.
We went there, then we came back here. I liked the back here part best.
I got bonked on the trip. Home is better when fewer things bonk me.
I thought following meant you were on my side. That was the important bit.
The boat helped. I will admit, being carried home by water is easier on the knees.
Crossing ocean by boat was a better idea than swimming it. Thank you for keeping me dry.
I crossed ocean water without a boat and still made it home. Next time, please find wood before waves.
The boat ride was the quiet part. Getting hurt before or after it spoiled the memory.
The ocean crossing by boat was manageable. The part where I got hurt was less impressive.
Swimming across ocean and coming home hurt is not an adventure I want repeated.
You put me in a boat, took me along, and then broke trust. Strange journey, worse ending.
A boat is honest enough. It goes where it is pointed, unlike some plans.
A boat carries armor poorly, but it carried me well enough.
I prefer a steady block beneath me, but the boat got us back without carving a new problem.
I could chart that boat route. I might add a warning mark beside it.
The boat floated. My nerves, less so. Still, I am home.
I know soil better than water. The boat was appreciated.
The boat drifted, but it did not miss the mark entirely.
Boat spray is poor treatment for leather. Better than swimming, though.
If I write that boat ride down, I will shelve it under anxious transportation.
No foundation under a boat, yet somehow it held. I respect the craft.
Keeping me in the boat was the hard part. I have chased calmer sheep.
That boat was the right tool for the crossing. I will give you that.
A boat is not armor, but it kept danger at a decent distance.
I learned I am not ready for a career in boating. But I survived the lesson.
The boat moved and I did not have to. I liked that part.
Remember when you made me follow you across {follow_biome}? I still know that road by ache alone.
Remember when you made me follow you over {follow_distance} blocks? My legs complained for days.
Remember when you took me along in a boat? I was not sure whether to thank you or ask where the oars had gone.
Remember when you took me across ocean water without a boat? I remember every splash.
That boat trip was part of a {follow_distance} block outing. Water did some of the work, but not enough.
Remember when I followed you and you hit me? I do. Still hurts.
I remember following you home hurt. I was grateful, but not exactly comfortable.
That trip through {follow_biome} tested my buckles more than most customers do.
Armor is not made for sitting in a boat. I learned that while following you.
When you had me follow you, I kept thinking the whole walk needed a sharper plan.
That boat route would look peaceful on a map. The lived version was wetter.
I could map the route you dragged me along, but I would mark several parts as questionable.
I have prayed about that time I followed you and you struck me. The bruise answered first.
You taking me by boat was almost sensible. Almost.
You remember that walk through {follow_biome}? I have tilled softer ground than that road.
I still remember that boat trip. Wet leather complains longer than villagers do.
Following you over {follow_distance} blocks felt like reeling in a boot with opinions.
That route you took me on flew about as straight as a warped arrow.
That boat ride was calm enough, until I remembered I was trusting you with the shore.
I still think about that walk. My boots forgave you before my feet did.
The story of me following you needs editing. Mostly shorter chapters and fewer hazards.
After following you that far, I understood why roads need better foundations.
When I followed you through {follow_biome}, I finally understood why sheep wander off quietly.
That time I followed you, the whole plan could have used a better handle.
Remember when I followed you and you hit me? Poor weapon discipline. Worse friendship.
I followed you once and learned something: I need better shoes before I choose a trade.
Remember when I followed you? I thought we were going somewhere. We sure did.
Remember the boat? I sat down and the world moved. Very clever.
A boat ride is better than being dragged over rough ground. Still, I prefer cutting across town, not water.
I said a quiet prayer during that boat ride. Mostly for balance.
Boats are not much like fields. No furrows, no rows, just water deciding if it likes you.
That boat did not fly straight, but at least it floated straight enough.
The boat chapter of our journey was damp, brief, and badly footnoted.
I do not trust anything with no foundation, but that boat held better than I expected.
A boat is just a tool with a nervous floor. Yours worked, mostly.
That boat trip had one good quality: no one was swinging steel in it.
I followed you into a boat once. Not a trade, apparently, but it felt like training.
The ocean crossing by boat would make a fine blue line on a map. I would label it 'questionable judgment.'
If we had to cross ocean, at least you used a boat. That is the first sensible part of the story.
Swimming across ocean with you was not fishing. It was being the catch.
Ocean swimming is terrible for leather and worse for my mood.
It held when trouble came close. That matters more than shine.
I had to trust it in a fight. I am glad you thought ahead.
The {gear_kind} earned its place. I noticed that more than I expected.
When it mattered, I was better prepared than I would have been alone.
I have not needed it yet. That is the best kind of preparation.
It is ready. I would rather carry caution than regret.
The {gear_kind} is still waiting. I hope it stays that way.
I have not had to use it. Still, walking home feels a little easier.
It took the moment cleanly. Good gear is quiet until the blow lands.
No dents yet. I can live with careful work staying untested.
It found its purpose. I prefer tools that know when to stop.
Still sharp, still waiting. That is better than needing it twice.
It kept its line under pressure. A steady hand is easier with proper tools.
I used it and did not drop it. That is two victories, if you ask me.
It handled ugly work without making a mess of me. I count that as fine quality.
Still clean. That is how I prefer tools before the hard work starts.
It helped me keep my bearings when the road stopped feeling safe.
Unused so far. A good map and good gear both matter most before trouble starts.
It bought me the breath I needed. Sometimes protection is its own blessing.
I have not needed it. I will still be grateful before I am desperate.
It kept me standing. Crops recover faster when the farmer does too.
Unused, thankfully. I would rather wear out a hoe than this.
It held steady. Better than most nets, and those are meant to catch trouble.
Dry, unused, and welcome. Some things should stay out of the water and out of danger.
Still unused. A ready shot is not wasted just because it stays in the quiver.
It flexed where it should and held where it had to. Good work saves skin.
No scuffs yet. I appreciate gear that does not rush to prove itself.
It performed as promised. I may need to revise my opinion of practical gifts upward.
Untested. I have filed it under things I hope remain theoretical.
Solid work. It took the pressure like good stone in the right wall.
Still unmarked. Strong things do not need to boast before the load comes.
It helped keep the wolves from making a story of me. That is enough praise.
Unused so far. I prefer watching over nervous sheep to testing nervous steel.
It did its job without complaint. That is the highest compliment a tool gets.
Still ready. A tool can be useful before it ever bites into work.
It helped. Maybe being ready is a profession of its own for now.
Unused so far. I may not have a trade, but I know preparation when I see it.
I have not used it. I have practiced looking brave with it, which is almost something.
We saw what you did when the raiders came. People count that sort of courage carefully.
The bell rang and you ran toward the danger. That is not nothing.
You helped. I know that. I am still hearing the horns in my head.
Maybe you saved us. Maybe I need another day before I can say that without shaking.
You stood where armor matters most. I respect that more than clean talk.
You held when the gate needed holding. Armor is easier to trust after seeing that.
I know the smell of fear and smoke. You pushed both back from our doors.
There are clean cuts and ugly fights. That was ugly, but you helped finish it.
I marked where the raiders came through. I also marked where you turned them back.
Maps make borders look calm. You reminded me borders have to be defended.
I prayed for courage in the village. It seems some of it found you.
Every life still here is a quieter bell than the one that rang. Thank you.
They trampled the rows, but not the village. You had a hand in that.
We will still have a harvest because there are still hands to gather it.
When trouble came in like a bad tide, you helped drag it back out.
A village is a harbor in its own way. You kept ours from burning.
I heard arrows, axes, shouting. Then I saw you still standing for us.
Good aim is choosing what matters under pressure. You chose the village.
A few straps snapped and a few nerves did too, but the village held.
Leather remembers every cut. So do people. This one may be remembered kindly.
I intend to write this down accurately. You stood with us when it mattered.
Some deeds deserve more than a margin note. Yours may be one of them.
Walls help, but walls do not swing back. You did.
A village stands on more than stone. Yesterday, it stood on nerve.
I ducked very professionally. You did the scarier part, which was nice.
The horn went bwaa and everyone ran. You ran the useful direction.
A frightened flock scatters. A frightened village nearly does too. You helped gather us.
I can mend torn wool. Mending a village takes people who show up.
Good hands under pressure are rare. Yours were useful when the village needed them.
A tool proves itself under strain. So did you.
I am still finding my place here. You made sure there was a here to find it in.
I had no station, no trade, just a door to hide behind. You kept that door standing.
A weapon means little without the nerve to use it at the gate. You had that nerve.
You kept your edge when the village lost its breath. That deserves respect.
I hear you. I have not forgotten, but I hear you.
An apology is a start. Let your hands prove the rest.
Words mend less than actions, but I will remember that you said them.
Thank you for saying it plainly. Do better by us, and this can pass.
Okay. I am still telling someone older, though.
Fine. I know what can be repaired. I also know what keeps the dent.
I will loosen the straps a little. Earn the rest with what you do next.
That was bluntly said. Good. Blunt is better than pretending nothing happened.
I clean up messes for a living. This one is yours to clean properly.
I can mark the apology. Whether the route changes is up to you.
Some paths can be corrected after a bad turn. Do not make me redraw this one twice.
Remorse is useful only if it changes the next choice. I hope yours does.
Repentance is not a speech. It is a repair repeated until trust returns.
An apology is a seed. It still needs watering, and I will be watching the crop.
Break a fence and you mend it before night. Trust works much the same.
You cast trouble into the water. Fine. Now reel back something better.
Bad tides pass. I will see whether you bring the same storm again.
Straight words are worth more than crooked excuses. Keep them straight.
You missed the mark badly. The apology lands closer. Do not waste it.
A clean stitch still leaves a seam. I accept the stitch. I remember the cut.
Hard things can soften with work. Start there.
I will file that apology carefully. The follow-up is the part worth reading.
I will not erase the record. I may add this to it.
Cracks spread if ignored. You noticed this one. Now prove you can patch it.
Mortar takes time to set. So does forgiveness.
That sounded sorry. I am still standing over here for a bit.
I accept the apology, but I am keeping one pocket full of suspicion.
I count losses carefully. I can count an apology too, if it is real.
Rough hands ruin good wool. Gentle choices from here, yes?
A bent tool can be reworked, if the metal is worth saving. Show me yours is.
Words are the handle. Actions are the head. I need both before I trust the tool.
I am trying to belong here. Please do not make that harder.
Fine. We can start again from here, but not from before.
A weapon is honest about harm. People should try being that honest before causing it.
Good. Now keep your temper sheathed unless the village needs it drawn.
I did. Still breathing, still standing. That counts for more than it sounds.
Back to the village in one piece. I will remember who helped make that true.
A few new dents, no missing plates. That is a victory I can repair.
I have handled sharp nights before. This one nearly handled me back.
I could draw the route back with my eyes closed. I would rather not walk it again tonight.
A little faith, a little medicine, and a very fast prayer. Yes, I made it back.
Fields teach patience. Fights teach exactly when patience has run out.
I have pulled mean things from dark water. Tonight was louder, that is all.
Lost two arrows, kept my nerve. I will call that a fair trade.
Scratches, scuffs, and one strap I do not trust anymore. Nothing I cannot mend.
I prefer danger in books. Books usually stay on the correct side of the shelf.
Stone chips, tools chip, people chip too. Important thing is not breaking.
I made it back because I ran exactly the clever amount. No one measures that.
I have chased enough trouble from the flock to know when trouble has teeth.
Good tools held. So did I. I will inspect both before sleeping.
I do not have a trade for that sort of night. I survived it anyway.
The blade did its work, and so did my feet when it was time to come home.
Every buckle held except the one in my knees. I will forgive that one.
Still here, still got all my fingers, still not eager to repeat it.
For a moment, every direction looked wrong. Then home looked possible again.
I kept one candle burning and one foot moving. Somehow both worked.
Mud on my boots, fear in my throat, and home still ahead. I made it.
I followed the safest current I could find. Tonight, that current was back here.
My quiver is lighter, but so is my heart now that I am inside the village again.
Wore half the sole off one boot getting back. Worth it.
There were several endings I disliked. I am glad we reached this chapter.
My hands shook too much to hold a chisel after. Still, they held long enough.
I only ran the wrong way once, maybe twice, and then I found the right door.
I know the sound of everyone trying to get through one gate at once. I made it through.
My grip held when it had to. I will think about that for a while.
I found a corner, then a path, then home. That is more plan than I started with.
Heat, pressure, fear. Good steel survives that. So did I.
My hands still keep checking straps that are already there. I made it back, though.
The plates held, the straps held, and somehow I held too.
I will hammer out the dents tomorrow. Tonight I am grateful there is a tomorrow.
Armor can turn a blow, but it cannot quiet the heart after. I am home, at least.
I counted every buckle at the door. All present. That felt like a blessing.
A few marks on the metal, a few in my memory. Nothing missing.
I came back with a shaking hand and an empty stomach. Better than not coming back.
There was too much noise and not enough door between me and it. I found the door.
I have had hard mornings, but that night was something else entirely.
My apron has seen worse stains. My nerves have not.
I made it home, and I am counting that before I count anything else.
The cleaver stayed in my grip. So did my sense, barely.
I know the way home on paper. Knowing it while scared is different.
Every landmark looked strange in the dark. Then the village lights found me.
I would mark that route in red if I ever had to draw it.
The map says the road is short. My feet disagree.
I came back with no new map, only a better respect for old paths.
For once, I was glad the village was exactly where I left it.
I returned with a prayer half-finished and gratitude fully earned.
My hands shook too much for the bell afterward, but I was alive to hear it.
There are nights that make faith very practical. I survived one.
I kept repeating the same blessing until my feet reached home.
The altar looked brighter after that road back.
I made it, though my voice may need a quiet hour.
I made it back with mud on my knees and luck in both pockets.
The field path never felt so long. The village never looked so good.
I kept thinking about sunrise. That helped me keep moving.
I have weathered storms, but storms do not usually carry axes.
Home was the only crop I cared about reaching.
My boots are ruined. I am not. Good trade.
I followed the sound of home like a line pulled tight.
Dark water is honest compared to a dark road with raiders near it.
I came back cold, winded, and happy to complain about both.
The night tried to pull me under. I kept my head up.
I have lost catches before. I am glad I was not the catch this time.
The door felt like a dock after bad weather.
I counted arrows until counting steps mattered more.
My hands remembered what to do before my head caught up.
I made it back with an empty quiver and a full respect for walls.
The road home felt like a target I could barely see.
A steady breath is harder when the dark is shouting.
I lost my aim for a moment. I did not lose the way home.
My boots earned every scuff getting back here.
I will be stitching straps until sunrise, but I am here to stitch them.
The night pulled hard. Good seams held.
I came home with scratches, not silence. I prefer scratches.
One sole nearly split and my courage nearly followed. Both held.
I can mend the gear. The shaking may take longer.
I made it back with several new reasons to prefer quiet shelves.
That chapter had too much running and not enough punctuation.
I survived, though my notes from the event are mostly shaking lines.
The village door has never looked so beautifully constructed.
I would shelve that experience under never again.
Home is a short word. It felt very large when I reached it.
I made it back chipped around the edges, but not broken.
Stone dust in my sleeves, fear in my teeth, home under my feet.
A wall looks different after you have wished for one.
I kept moving one step at a time. That is how anything solid gets built.
The road tried to crack me. It failed.
I will trust walls more tomorrow. Tonight I trust doors.
I survived by making several choices very quickly and only some of them silly.
The door was exactly where I hoped it was. Eventually.
I came back alive, which is my favorite kind of back.
I was brave for at least three seconds. The rest was very fast walking.
Someone shouted run, and I became excellent at listening.
I made it home and only lost one thought on the way.
I counted my steps back like I count heads at dusk.
A scattered mind is hard to gather. I managed it enough to get home.
The village gate felt like a pen after a long, bad storm.
I made it back with my heart running ahead of me.
Keeping calm is easier when no one is shouting. I did my best anyway.
I reached home and only then remembered to breathe properly.
The handle held, the edge held, and I held on behind them.
I will inspect every tool I carried. I may inspect my knees too.
A good grip saved me more than once tonight.
I made it back with work to do and hands still able to do it.
Nothing tests a tool like fear. Nothing tests a person faster.
I know what stress does to metal now. I know what it does to me too.
I made it back without a trade, a plan, or much dignity. Still counts.
I learned that I am very motivated by closed doors and warm lights.
Home looked like the best job I could possibly have.
I survived by following people who seemed less confused than I was.
I reached the village and decided that was enough achievement for the day.
I have no title for what I did. I lived through it.
Steel sang, fear shouted, and I still heard the way home.
I kept my blade ready and my feet smarter than pride.
No weapon feels heavy until you carry it back after the fight.
I survived with the edge intact and the lesson sharper.
I trust good steel. Tonight I had to trust my own nerve too.
The fight ended before I did. That is the result I prefer.
I can repair damage when someone brings it to the anvil. You have brought yours.
Do not mistake acceptance for softness. I heard you, and I will be watching.
A dent tells me where the strike landed. Your apology tells me you know it landed.
Words are light. Better choices have weight. Bring those next.
I will set this aside for now, not throw it away.
Fine. Let the next thing you make be trust, not trouble.
I prefer clean cuts to messy words. That was clean enough to hear.
You made a mess. Start by not making another one.
An apology does not put things back on the hook, but it is a beginning.
I will take the words. I will judge the hands.
Fine. Say it once, then prove it every time after.
I know when something has gone bad. This does not have to.
You are asking to redraw a line you crossed. That can be done carefully.
A bad route is not shameful if you correct it before others follow.
I will mark this apology, but not as the destination.
Do not make a habit of needing a way back from harm.
Fine. Let us see whether your next steps match your words.
Some mistakes become warnings on maps. Try not to become one.
Contrition is a door. Walk through it, do not stand in front of it.
I accept the words. Make the next act worthy of them.
Mercy is not forgetfulness. It is a chance to choose better.
A wounded trust heals slowly. Still, healing can begin here.
If remorse has roots, we will see fruit.
I will hold this apology with care. Do not make it lonely.
You stepped on trust like young shoots. It can grow back if you stop trampling it.
Fine. Plant better behavior where that harm was.
I will not pull up the apology before it sprouts. Do not let it wither.
A fence mended poorly breaks again. Mend this properly.
Words are rain. Useful, but not enough by themselves.
I have seen hard ground soften. Maybe you can too.
You tangled the line. Fine. Untangle it slowly and do not cut it again.
An apology floats. Trust sinks or holds by what follows.
I will hear you out. I have waited longer for worse catches.
Bad waters calm if the wind changes. Let us see whether yours does.
You hooked harm and brought it here. Now bring something decent.
Fine. I will not throw the words back, but I will inspect them.
The apology flies straighter than the harm did. That is something.
Do not notch the same mistake twice.
I hear the words. Now keep your aim away from us.
A bent shaft can be corrected if it has not split. Prove you have not split.
Fine. Let this be the shot you meant to take.
Trust is easy to miss and hard to hit again. Try carefully.
Trust is not leather, but it still stretches thin when treated badly.
Fine. Let us see whether your next touch is gentler.
You made a tear. The apology is a needle, not the whole repair.
I will accept the first stitch. Keep sewing.
Rough handling leaves marks. I heard you admit that.
Do not pull at a mending place before it has strength.
Your apology is noted. The revision will be in your behavior.
I dislike repeat offenses in any edition.
Words can clarify. They cannot replace the missing page.
I will not close the book on you yet. Do not make me regret the bookmark.
The statement is clear. The evidence must follow.
I accept the correction. Now avoid making an errata list.
You made a crack. You named it. That is the first proper repair.
Do not plaster over this and call it fixed.
Fine. A foundation can be reset, but it takes honest work.
I hear the apology. Now bring mortar, not dust.
Damage hidden inside stone still spreads. Keep this in the open.
Trust can stand again if the base is not shaken twice.
That sounded like the right kind of sorry. I think.
I accept, but I am standing behind this idea of distance for now.
Okay. Try doing the good version of that next time.
I will forgive a bit now and maybe another bit after lunch.
Words received. Suspicion still lightly worn.
Fine. I am putting the apology somewhere safe in my head.
A frightened heart remembers rough handling. Be gentler from here.
Fine. I will count the apology, but I will also count what follows.
Trust scatters quickly. Gather it patiently.
Do not chase forgiveness. Walk steady and let it come closer.
I hear you. Keep your hands calm around this village.
Words can be soft. Make your choices soft too.
A poor strike can ruin good work. Learn control before you swing again.
Fine. Rework the habit, not just the sentence.
I accept the apology as raw material. Make something better from it.
Do not bring me another broken trust and ask why it failed.
Words set the handle. Actions drive the head tight.
If you mean it, the next repair starts now.
I am still figuring out where I fit. Please do not make me fit around fear.
Fine. I accept, but I need room to believe it.
That helps. Not everything, but it helps.
I do not have a profession for judging apologies. This one sounds real enough to start.
Let us call this a beginning, not a finish.
I will give the apology a place. Give me a reason to keep it there.
Harm is easy to make and hard to take back. At least you know which you did.
Fine. Keep the sharp parts of yourself pointed where they belong.
An apology is not a sheath, but it may keep the edge from cutting twice.
I respect honest remorse more than polished excuses.
If you cannot control your hand, no apology will be enough. Control it.
Good. Let this be the last time I hear that tone for this reason.
You fought like someone who understands what a door is worth.
I saw you stand between iron and panic. That stays with me.
The village needed a shield before the walls did. You were one.
Good armor is not only worn. Sometimes it arrives carrying a weapon.
When the shouting started, you did not fold. I respect that.
You gave the village time to breathe. Every guard knows the value of time.
You kept the raid from reaching more kitchens than mine. I noticed.
The village smelled of smoke and fear. Then it smelled like survival.
You did hard work when hard work was needed. That matters.
I saw raiders turn from our doors because you were there.
No one wants that kind of fight, but someone had to answer it.
You helped keep families at their tables. That is worth saying aloud.
I can point to where you met them. That spot feels different now.
A village border is not ink. Yesterday, you made that clear.
You changed the shape of the danger before it reached the center.
I marked the raid path. I also marked where it stopped.
The map of this place has one more reason to keep its name.
You made the distance between raiders and homes matter.
I prayed for protection and saw someone answer with action.
You gave fear less room inside these walls.
The bell called for help, and you came before the echo faded.
There are blessings spoken and blessings done. Yours was done.
I will remember the courage, even while I tend the frightened.
The village is quieter because you helped end the noise.
The fields can be replanted. The people had to be kept alive first.
You helped make sure we still have hands for the harvest.
Raiders came for more than crops. You stopped them short.
I saw you fighting near the rows. That is not forgotten.
You kept the village standing long enough for morning chores to matter.
The ground remembers heavy boots. I will remember who drove them off.
The raid came in rough, and you helped break the current.
You kept the danger from dragging more of us under.
I saw you stand where the tide was meanest.
A safe harbor takes work. Yesterday, you did some.
The village rode out the storm because people held fast.
You helped haul the worst of that night away from our doors.
You picked the right target when the raid pressed in.
I saw you move where the arrows were pointing. That takes nerve.
The village needed steady aim, and you gave it more than words.
Every raider stopped early is a home spared late.
You helped turn the fight before it reached the center.
I respect anyone who can choose clearly while the air is full of panic.
You helped keep more than roofs intact. People held together because of it.
The village came through worn, but not torn apart.
I saw courage stretched tight and not snapping. Yours included.
Raiders test every weak point. You became a strong one.
I can repair gear. You helped spare things that cannot be repaired as easily.
The doors, straps, and nerves all held better because you fought.
The account will say you came when the village needed help.
I saw a story turn because someone chose not to flee.
There are records of raids and records of people who stopped them. You earned a line.
The village archive remains intact. So do we, thanks in part to you.
I will remember the facts: danger came, and you answered.
Some deeds sound exaggerated until one sees them from a doorway.
The wall held better because someone stood beyond it.
You gave the village another layer of stone when it needed one.
I saw raiders hit our edge and fail to break through.
Good work under pressure keeps structures standing. So does courage.
The village is still square on its foundation because people held firm.
You helped keep the center from cracking.
You ran toward the loud part. That seemed important and extremely bold.
I was under a table, but I heard useful fighting. Yours, probably.
The village is still here, and I am very attached to that outcome.
You made the raiders stop doing raid things near us. Excellent choice.
I did morale from a safe place. You did the dangerous part.
When the horn sounded, you became part of the answer. I liked that.
You helped keep panic from scattering everyone beyond reach.
The village needed gathering, and your courage gave us a center.
I saw people find their doors because the raiders were forced back.
A safe fold matters most when the night is loud.
You helped bring the village through frightened but together.
Some courage is quiet afterward. I see it anyway.
You were the right tool in a terrible moment.
When pressure came down, you did not warp.
The village needed more than sharp edges. It needed steady hands.
You made yourself useful where usefulness mattered most.
I saw the kind of work no bench can teach.
Good work leaves marks. Yours left people alive to notice.
I do not have much here yet, but you helped keep what I might become part of.
The village still has room for me because people like you fought for it.
I had nowhere important to stand, so I watched. You stood somewhere important.
You protected more than houses. You protected chances.
I saw a future here look less certain, then you pushed back.
Maybe I will find work tomorrow because there is still a village tomorrow.
You used force for the village, not against it. That distinction matters.
I saw discipline in that fight. Not just fury.
Raiders understand strength. Yesterday, so did you.
You met danger at the edge and kept it from cutting deeper.
A blade is judged by what it protects. People are too.
You fought clean enough for me to respect the work.
I found a really good hiding place, but I cannot tell you or it stops being good.
The bell is loud up close. I learned that by mistake.
Hi again!
I can say hello from here.
A question? I know three things: doors, bells, and which path has puddles.
Ask a grown-up. They like sounding certain.
Once I ran all the way around the well and did not fall in. That is the whole story, but it was very exciting.
I had a dream I was tall enough to see over every fence.
Why did the bell ring? Because it had something important to say!
If I stand very still, chores cannot see me.
That was not nice.
You are being scary.
The paths tell you plenty if you watch who hurries and who lingers.
Trust is built from small things. Villages are very good at counting small things.
Once the bell rang for a wandering cat. Everyone still claims they were not scared.
I still remember that {attack_weapon}. Conversations get colder after that.
The bell has been quiet today. I would like to keep it that way.
The square tells you who is busy, who is worried, and who is pretending not to be either.
Why do we shut doors early? Because night makes ordinary mistakes harder to fix.
One season, half the village learned roofing because the rain would not stop teaching.
I know an emerald joke, but it costs extra if you want the good part.
You walk like the path owes you an apology.
Most village work is simple until everyone depends on it being done right.
What do villagers remember? More than visitors hope, less than rumors claim.
The well once went dry for a morning, and suddenly every bucket had a reputation.
It is hard to speak plainly while remembering that {attack_weapon}.
{gift_item} is usually welcome. Simple, useful gifts travel well.
Most villagers would be glad to receive {gift_item}.
If you are unsure, {gift_item} is a kind choice.
A gift like {gift_item} says you came with good intentions.
Villagers remember practical kindness. {gift_item} counts.
A village can usually find room for {gift_item}.
For most villagers, {gift_item} is worth a smile.
{gift_item} makes a good peaceable gift.
Bring {gift_item} and most villagers will understand the gesture.
{gift_item} is welcome more often than not.
{gift_item} makes a poor gift. Most villagers would rather not handle it.
{gift_item} sends the wrong message.
If you are trying to be kind, avoid {gift_item}.
{gift_item} is more warning than present.
Handing someone {gift_item} is a quick way to sour the room.
{gift_item} belongs somewhere else, not in someone's hands as a gift.
Most people here would call {gift_item} a bad offering.
Better to arrive empty-handed than with {gift_item}.
Do not wrap {gift_item} and call it kindness.
{gift_item} is the kind of gift people remember for the wrong reason.
If you are choosing for {gift_subject}, {gift_item} is a thoughtful pick.
For {gift_subject}, {gift_item} shows you paid attention.
{gift_subject} can make good use of {gift_item}.
{gift_item} suits {gift_subject} better than most gifts.
You can tell someone knows the trade when they bring {gift_item}.
That work gives {gift_item} real value.
{gift_item} is the kind of thing {gift_subject} remembers kindly.
A careful gift for {gift_subject}? {gift_item}.
{gift_subject} tends to respect a gift like {gift_item}.
{gift_item} feels personal to {gift_subject}.
If you are choosing for {gift_subject}, I would avoid {gift_item}.
For {gift_subject}, {gift_item} feels careless.
Do not bring {gift_item} to {gift_subject} and expect gratitude.
{gift_subject} has little use for {gift_item}.
{gift_item} is a poor match for {gift_subject}.
If I were gifting {gift_subject}, I would leave {gift_item} at home.
{gift_subject} may take {gift_item} the wrong way.
For that profession, {gift_item} is more nuisance than gift.
You can insult the trade without meaning to. {gift_item} may do it.
{gift_item} is the kind of thing {gift_subject} remembers sourly.
I think you already know what I can tell you about gifts.
You've picked my memory clean on gifts, I'm afraid.
No fresh advice. Try another villager if you want more gift gossip.
I would rather not pretend I know more than I do.
No new gift advice from me today. Ask someone else and you may hear more.
That is the end of my gift wisdom for the moment.
Nothing new comes to mind. Gifts are personal, even when villagers gossip.
I do not have another gift tip ready for you.
I remember pieces. Your face came back before my voice did. Thank you for waiting on the other side.
I remember enough to know you pulled me out of something dark.
I know you, I think. The memory has teeth marks around the edges.
Your voice sounds familiar, but everything before the cure is fog and hunger.
I remember you. That does not make the remembering easy.
Word reached us about {cured_villager}. You brought one of ours back.
{cured_villager_possessive} cure matters here. People remember who stayed to help.
I heard you cured {cured_villager}. That is not a small thing.
{cured_villager} is walking these paths again because of you. The village noticed.
I heard what you did for {cured_villager}. I am still wary, but I will not pretend that meant nothing.
Helping {cured_villager} speaks well of you. It does not erase everything else.
You saved {cured_villager}. I know. I just do not know what to do with both that and the rest.
Are you the doctor who saved {cured_villager}?
The grown-ups said you are the wizard that saved {cured_villager}. Are you really?
The thunder shook everyone, but the village is still standing.
We are rattled, not broken. Count heads before counting damage.
The little ones jumped at every crack, but most doors held.
Lightning makes honest fear out of everyone. Thank you for asking.
We are checking roofs, bells, and nerves after that thunder.
The sky was so loud. I stayed near the bed and did not like it.
I think everyone is okay, but the thunder made my knees feel funny.
The grown-ups said stay inside. I stayed very inside.
I counted the booms and lost count because I hid.
Nobody should let the sky shout that much.
The smoke has thinned, but everyone is still counting what was lost.
We put out what we could. Keep water close until the smell fades.
Fire leaves more than ash. People will be jumpy for a while.
No one wants to say they were scared first, so I will: we were scared.
Everyone is checking walls, beds, and each other after the flames.
There was smoke and grown-ups yelling. I stayed low like they said.
I do not like fire when it runs around loose.
Someone carried water very fast. I tried to help by not being in the way.
The air tasted bad, but I think everyone found a safe place.
I am okay. My blanket smells smoky though.
The raid is over for now. Some of us are still listening for horns.
Everyone alive is accounted for, but calm takes longer to return.
We barred the doors, held our breath, and made it to the other side.
Ask again after the shaking stops. For now, yes, most are safe.
The bell did its work. So did the brave ones. The rest of us remember.
The bell was loud and everyone ran. I ran too.
I hid where I was told. I think that means I helped.
The bad people are gone, right? Please say they are gone.
I heard shouting outside and did not peek. Not even once.
My heart is still running even though my feet stopped.
The night brought trouble, but dawn found us still here.
We are checking doors and wounds. Night makes every sound suspicious now.
Some slept through it. Some will not sleep well for a while.
The attack passed, but people are keeping lamps lit anyway.
Everyone is quieter after a bad night. Quiet can mean alive, at least.
I heard monsters and pulled the blanket over my head.
Night was too noisy. I want morning to stay longer.
Someone told me not to open the door, so I did not.
I am okay, but I want the lamps left on.
The dark made bad sounds. The grown-ups made braver sounds.
The wind came in hard enough to make the whole village taste like dust.
No rain here, just grit in the shutters and everyone checking their eyes.
The sand got everywhere, but people found their way indoors.
Harsh wind can scare a village nearly as well as thunder. We are still here.
We are sweeping doorways and counting heads after that wall of dust.
The wind threw sand at the windows. I did not like the sound.
I got dust in my mouth even inside. How does it do that?
The grown-ups said cover my face, so I did.
It was like the ground tried to fly away.
I am okay, but my hair feels crunchy.
The snow came down hard, but the hearths held and the doors stayed shut.
Cold frightens slowly. We are checking fingers, roofs, and firewood.
The village went white and quiet for a while. Quiet is not always peace.
Everyone is chilled, but accounted for. Warmth matters now.
We are clearing paths before the snow hides what people need.
The snow made everything disappear. I stayed where I could see a lantern.
My toes got cold just looking outside.
The wind pushed snow at the door like it wanted in.
I am okay. I want soup though.
The whole village looked like a blanket, but a scary blanket.

pacify.text: Fine. I will stand down, but peace takes more than emeralds.
I will let this pass for now. Do not make me regret it.
That is enough to cool my temper. Keep your hands peaceful.
That is not enough. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds} if you want this settled.
You are short. Peace costs {emerald_cost} {emeralds} today.
A small offer will not calm a large mistake. I need {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
No. Some things are not bought back with emeralds.
Keep them. I do not trust your apology.
The village remembers too much for that to work.
